newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein denies IRA "truce" conference report.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein denies IRA "truce" conference report.

text.p: Irish republican officials on Sunday dismissed reports that a conference planned for next month would be a front for a landmark convention at which IRA guerrilla fighters could agree to a new ceasefire.

British media raised hopes at the weekend the Irish Republican Army might be moving towards a new truce in its guerrilla war to end British rule in Northern Ireland by holding a historic "army convention", its first for ten years.

They said a conference on the state of the Irish language to be sponsored by the Irish Republican Army's political wing, Sinn Fein, could provide a venue for IRA guerrillas to decide the future of the IRA's bombing campaign.
But a Sinn Fein spokesman told Reuters: "We can reject any claim that this year's Slogadh (conference) is anything other than what it is - an Irish language conference."
"It is not a cover for the IRA. It is a public event open to Irish language activists and the media."

London's Sunday Times reported that British security sources felt that a rare IRA convention might be held soon to decide the future of a bombing campaign that is blocking Sinn Fein from a seat in multi-party peace talks.

The newspaper said that the language conference in Donegal in the Irish Republic on October 4 might be a venue for the IRA guerrillas to elect new leaders and bridge a dangerous gulf between hawks and doves.
The IRA, one of the world's olded guerrilla armies with huge stockpiles of arms and explosives, abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February with a string of bombing attacks on mainland Britain.

Britain and Ireland, joint sponsors of multi-party talks that are poised for a further fractious session on Monday, are adamant that the IRA must call off hostilities before Sinn Fein is allowed to the table.
The multi-party talks started in June under the chairmanship of former U.S. senator George Mitchell, but diagreements on issues of procedure have held up progress to date.
The new speculation about an IRA convention comes on the heels of optimistic comments by Irish Prime Minister John Bruton about prospects for a truce.

During a visit to the United States last week, Bruton said he thought an IRA cessation could be on the cards if the two powerful political parties in the region - the Ulster Unionists supported by majority pro-British Protestants and moderate Social Democratic and Labour supported by most Catholcs - make headway in easing difficulties plaguing the talks process.

Founded in 1916, and supported in fiercely pro-Irish Catholic enclaves in Northern Ireland, the IRA has launched many campaigns against British forces, the most violent lasting 25 years until its truce in September 1994. REUTER
